doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Adapting to the audience and playing Small's
summary: He changes his playing for crowds and rooms, and plays Small's with the trio Bop Juice.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Do you think you change your playing to fit certain different circumstances?

Oh yeah. I do. Oh I’m definitely influenced by the moment and by the place and by the environment. Oh sure. Definitely. Like if I was to play a concert for a bunch of old people let’s say, tunes I would pick I would play differently than I would play for, like I say a college crowd. Definitely. And even the club. Like I play Small’s a lot, Small’s.
It’s on, you can get that on video live, right?

Oh yes, that’s right. I’m usually there, one Saturday every month, at 7:30, yeah. And I play a trio, Bop Juice, it’s a trio, with Clifford Barbaro, and the bass player du jour and me. So it’s Bop Juice.
Yeah. Because you know bass players get too many gigs, so you know I have a bunch of guys I use.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. They work all the time so sometimes they can’t make 7:30 on a Saturday night.
Right. You start going down your list.
You know, some things are the same on any level.
That’s right. That’s right, sure, oh definitely. Well what was the question?
The question was altering your playing somewhat for different circumstances.

Yeah. I definitely do that. Yes. The crowd, yes. I mean that’s just the way I am. That’s just the way I see things. It’s like if you walked in a room and the President of the United States was here you would talk to him differently than if the janitor was here. Not that — I wouldn’t have any less respect for the janitor, but that’s the way I grew up, that’s the way my father was and is. He can talk to anybody about anything. So that’s my influence. But I would talk to him differently though.
